ref: DAR — Revelation ch. 21: The New Jerusalem
title: The New Jerusalem
voicePrompt: Explain in your own words Smith's central argument that the New Jerusalem is a literal city and the true 'bride, the Lamb's wife' — not the church — and walk through the evidence he gives (the angel's promise, the city's physical dimensions, and the marriage figure of Christ as Bridegroom, the city as bride, and believers as guests).

questions.stem: How does Smith use Revelation 21:1 to refute the claim that the Bible's 'third heaven' is merely a future third state of the present heavens and earth?
options: John reckons only two heavens and earths (calling the present ones the 'first'), so the future ones would be the second, not a third — proving Peter was not establishing a numerical order
John explicitly states there are exactly three heavens, matching Peter's count
John says the third heaven was destroyed by the flood
John denies that any heaven exists in the present time
questions.explanation: Smith argues that John 'here reckons but two heavens and earths,' calling the present ones 'the first,' so the future new heavens would be the second, not the third as Peter reckons. Hence Peter was not establishing a numerical order, and the 'third heaven' arguments against a literal present paradise fall to the ground.

questions.stem: What is Smith's interpretation of 'there was no more sea' in verse 1?
options: All seas are permanently abolished and there will never be a sea again
John speaks only of the present sea passing away; the old sea no longer appeared, and there may yet be a new sea as there is a new earth
The sea becomes the lake of fire
The sea is a symbol for the wicked nations being destroyed
questions.explanation: Smith says it does not certainly follow that there will be no sea; John speaks only of the present heaven, earth, and sea. The old sea 'no longer appeared, any more than the old heaven and old earth; and yet there may be a new sea as there is a new earth' — supported by the river of life needing somewhere to discharge and by Zechariah 9:10.

questions.stem: According to Smith, what does 'God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes' mean?
options: God literally wipes tears from each person's face one by one
There will be tears of joy that God dries
He wipes away tears by removing all causes of tears, since there will be no tears in that kingdom to be wiped away
The tears refer to the suffering of the wicked in the lake of fire
questions.explanation: Smith writes that God 'does not literally wipe away tears from the eyes of his people; for there will be no tears in that kingdom to be thus wiped away; but he wipes away tears by removing all causes of tears.'

questions.stem: Why does Smith insist the New Jerusalem cannot be the church but must be a literal city?
options: Because the city is invisible and the church is visible

Because it would be absurd to describe the church as lying foursquare with a wall, twelve gates, and four sides toward the points of the compass; and because Paul calls the city 'the mother of us all,' making the church its children
Because the church was not yet founded when John wrote
Because the city is made of gold and the church is made of people
questions.explanation: Smith argues it would be absurd to talk of the church as lying foursquare with a great high wall and twelve gates toward the four points of the compass. Moreover, Paul (Galatians 4:26) calls the city 'the mother of us all,' so the church is the children of the city, not the city itself — making it a literal city.

questions.stem: How does Smith arrange the marriage figure so that there is 'no confusion of parties'?
options: Christ is the Bridegroom, the city is the bride, and the church (believers) are the guests
The church is both the bride and the mother of the children
Christ is the bride and the city is the Bridegroom
The Father is the Bridegroom and the church is the bride
questions.explanation: Smith writes: 'Christ is represented as the Bridegroom, the city as the bride, and we, the church, as the guests. There is no confusion of parties here.' He contrasts this with the popular view that makes the church both mother and children, both bride and guests.

questions.stem: What do the twelve apostles' names on the foundations and the twelve tribes' names on the gates signify, per Smith?
options: That the city was built by Jews for Jews only
That the city has two separate sections, one for the old covenant and one for the new
That the apostles rank above the tribes in the kingdom
That it is a Christian (not Jewish) city, and that all the saved from both dispensations are reckoned as belonging to one of the twelve tribes, since all must enter through one of the twelve gates
questions.explanation: Smith says the apostles' names in the foundations 'show it to be a Christian and not a Jewish city,' while the tribes' names on the gates show that all the saved — from this dispensation and the former — are reckoned as belonging to one of the twelve tribes, since all must enter through one of these gates. This explains why Christians are called Israel.

questions.stem: How does Smith resolve whether the city is as high as it is long and broad (verse 16)?
options: The city is exactly 1,500 miles high to match its length
The Greek 'isos' (equal) can mean proportion, so the height was proportionate to length and breadth — not equal to them — freeing the city from disproportion
The height cannot be determined from the text at all
The wall's height of 144 cubits is the city's total height
questions.explanation: Smith argues the Greek word 'isos' can convey proportion (citing Liddell and Scott, Pickering, Greenfield). The height was 'proportionate to its length and breadth, and not that it was as high as it was long,' which 'frees the language from all ambiguity, and the city from all disproportion.' He notes the low wall (about 264 feet) would otherwise be insignificant beside a 375-mile-high city.

questions.stem: Why does Smith say there is no temple in the New Jerusalem, and why need the golden street not be literally transparent?
options: There is no temple because God forbids worship; the street is dull metal

There is no temple because sacrificial and mediatorial work will be forever past (God and the Lamb being the temple); the street need only be so highly polished as to reflect like a mirror, not literally see-through
The temple was destroyed by fire; the street is transparent so the saved can see hell beneath
There is no temple because the city is too small; the street is glass with no gold
questions.explanation: Smith explains the temple involved sacrifices and mediatorial work, which 'will be forever past' once the city is on earth, so 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it.' For the street, he says it need not be literally transparent — if it were, one would see the substratum beneath; rather, it is so highly polished as to reflect 'like the truest mirror,' producing a grand effect.
